articles.title: Beyond air power: How long-range missiles are reshaping the rules of war
articles.summary: Long-range precision strikes are rewriting the rules of warfare.
articles.body: Long-range precision strikes are rewriting the rules of warfare. As satellites, unmanned aerial systems (UAS) and sensors operating across different spectra expand commanders’ view of the battlefield, long-range stand-off weapons allow them to strike targets from a distance. At the centre of this shift are long-range rockets and missiles.These weapons came into sharp focus during the conflict involving Iran, the United States and Israel, where Tehran relied on its missile arsenal to project military power and defend its sovereignty. The US Army has also deployed its Precision Strike Missile (PrSM), which has a range of 500 km. US Central Command, responsible for the West Asian theatre, described a strike by the weapon as record-setting, although the exact coordinates and distance involved remain classified. This occurred despite the US and Israel having established air superiority over Iran and carrying out strikes on ground targets.For the US, long-range one-way cruise missiles have been a key opening weapon since the First Gulf War in 1991, used to "kick open the door" for subsequent operations. Washington has employed the tactic in campaigns in the Balkans, Afghanistan, the Second Gulf War, Libya, Syria and now Iran. Such weapons reduce the exposure of manned aircraft to enemy air defences.For Iran, whose antiquated air force was destroyed in the early days of the conflict, long-range rockets and missiles have provided the ability to strike targets far beyond its borders. Decades of sanctions have constrained its military, but its missile arsenal has allowed it to punch above its weight. By striking countries across the Persian Gulf, Iran has secured a credible role in the conflict despite lacking an effective air force. China and Russia, too, maintain extensive rocket forces capable of delivering conventional and strategic weapons.Operation Sindoor and the missile race in South AsiaDuring Operation Sindoor in May 2025, India used long-range missiles to strike terror targets in Muridke and Bahawalpur. As the conflict progressed, India deployed more of these weapons against Pakistani airbases, from Bholari in the south to Sargodha and Nur Khan in the north. The strikes helped bring the Pakistani air force to the ground and contributed to Pakistan suing for peace.Pakistan, meanwhile, fired missiles, rockets and drones at Indian military installations across Jammu and Kashmir, Punjab, Rajasthan and Gujarat. Almost all these weapons were intercepted or neutralised.One prominent case involved a Fatah-II missile reportedly aimed at the National Capital Region. It was brought down over Sirsa in Haryana, around 240 km northwest of New Delhi, on May 10. Debris was recovered in the area. The episode left Islamabad facing a question its military planners have been working to answer: how can conventional weapons strike Indian targets and get through its defences?Pakistan’s response has been to establish a new organisation. On August 13, 2025, Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif announced the creation of the Army Rocket Force Command (ARFC), a formation intended to oversee missiles following the conflict with India.Headed by a three-star general, the command consolidates conventional rocket and missile units from several formations and specialist detachments. The Fatah-I and Fatah-II systems were developed to provide conventional strike options. During the conflict, they were mobilised only when international pressure forced de-escalation, leaving Pakistan without conventional rungs on the escalation ladder and unable to wrest control of escalation from India. The new command is intended to address that gap.The change is about tactics as much as hardware. Pakistan’s surface-to-surface missiles were historically managed with a strategic, nuclear purpose in mind, while conventional rocket artillery remained with the army’s artillery arm. Its units respond to different commanders depending on their deployment.Centralising conventional systems under one command shortens the chain between decision-makers, including the Pakistan army chief, the rocket force commander and field units. This is intended to enable faster decisions and concentrated firepower.Inside Pakistan’s Army Rocket Force CommandDuring Op Sindoor, Pakistan realised that there was considerable space between the upper limit of conventional ground based contact war and lower limits of the nuclear threshold. A huge void surfaced in the conventional non contact kinetic domain, in which Pakistan had no capability to either defend or carry out any offensive operations. India exploited this space with the Brahmos much to the embarrassment of Pakistan by plastering 11 airfields. Creation of the Army Rocket Force Command equipped with missiles retrofitted with conventional warheads seeks to plug this gap to regain balance. Pakistan aims not only to close this gap but use this new capability to threaten to lower the nuclear threshold. However what is to be noted is that by creating this force, Pakistan has tacitly indicated that it cannot cross the nuclear threshold with its customary display of irrationality. India will have to focus on neutralizing this newfound capability of Pakistan through defensive and offensive means.The weapons expected to form the core of the new command largely belong to the Fatah family.The Fatah-I is a guided multiple rocket launcher designed for tactical targets at ranges of 70 to 140 km. The Fatah-II has a reported range of around 400 km and uses inertial navigation with satellite guidance. It was used in combat in 2025.On October 13, 2026, the Army Rocket Force Command test-launched the Fatah-2 Extended Range. Pakistan’s military describes it as a hypersonic ballistic missile, although no range has been announced for this version.Pakistan has also unveiled the supersonic Fatah-III and the Fatah-IV, a ground-launched cruise missile with a stated range of 750 km. Its arsenal also includes the A-100 multiple launch rocket system acquired from China. The A-100 is based on Russia’s Smerch rocket system, which India also operates.A Fatah-V with a reported range of around 1,000 km has been discussed in defence media, but its existence is unconfirmed. Reports also differ on whether the longer-range Shaheen, Ghauri and Babur missiles will come under the new command. One-way attack drones have also been described as part of its inventory.The creation of the ARFC raises an obvious question: how does it differ from Pakistan’s Strategic Plans Division (SPD), the secretariat and operational arm of the National Command Authority, which controls the country’s nuclear arsenal?The Pakistan army’s Strategic Forces Command operates nuclear-capable missiles under the SPD’s security framework. The ARFC, by contrast, is a separate army formation responsible for conventional rockets and missiles, primarily those with short to medium ranges.The distinction is intended to allow Pakistan to signal conventional retaliation without immediately crossing the nuclear threshold. This has long complicated the deterrence equation between Islamabad and New Delhi.However, the separation is not complete and creates its own challenges. The SPD also oversees employment and deployment control committees that keep nuclear and conventional missiles ready. Establishing a new command means duplicating some of this work, along with the infrastructure, communications systems and trained personnel required.Reports have also indicated that Pakistan’s defence production, organised around entities linked to the division, is geared towards low-rate production of strategic assets rather than the large conventional quantities a rocket force would require. How effectively the two organisations coordinate during a crisis will be crucial.India’s expanding strike capabilityIndia has been strengthening its conventional strike capability since before Operation Sindoor. The army has inducted the Pinaka, Smerch, Pralay and BrahMos systems for different operational requirements.Pralay is a solid-propellant, quasi-ballistic missile with a reported range of 150 to 500 km. It has a manoeuvrable re-entry vehicle and carries a conventional warhead. The defence ministry cleared around 120 missiles in 2022, and Pralay completed back-to-back user trials in July 2025.The next iteration of BrahMos is expected to have a range of up to 800 km. Meanwhile, a long-range guided rocket version of the Pinaka, currently under development, is intended to reach targets up to 120 km away.India is also working on subsonic land-attack cruise missiles, including the Long-Range Land Attack Cruise Missile. It is expected to be cheaper than BrahMos and deployed in significantly larger numbers.The rationale is practical. The army has traditionally relied on the air force for deep strikes against command centres, ammunition dumps, bridges and logistics hubs. But modern air defences can engage targets hundreds of kilometres away. During Operation Sindoor, India’s S-400 surface-to-air missile system demonstrated this reach by bringing down a Pakistani aircraft from more than 300 km away.Sending fighter aircraft into heavily contested airspace can be costly. Missiles can strike many of these targets while leaving fighters available for other missions, an important consideration for an air force facing an acute shortage of squadrons.The missile shieldDuring the conflict, India’s integrated air defence network played a central role in defending military installations. The Integrated Air Command and Control System links radars and sensors with air defence units along the border.Pakistan targeted numerous military locations in northern and western India, but India’s layered defence network, comprising the S-400, Barak-8 or MR-SAM, Akash and counter-drone systems, held.India signed a Rs 35,000-crore deal for five S-400 squadrons in 2018, and three squadrons were operational by the time of the conflict. Sources said the S-400, Akash-NG and MR-SAM were capable of intercepting a missile such as the Fatah-II. However, India has not officially confirmed which system carried out the interception.The shield is now being expanded. In his Independence Day speech in August 2025, Prime Minister Narendra Modi announced Mission Sudarshan Chakra, an integrated, multilayered defence shield intended to be in place by 2035.A key component of its long-range defence architecture is Project Kusha, an extended-range air defence system designed to fill the gap between the MR-SAM and S-400. It is planned to have three interceptors with ranges of 150 km, 250 km and 350 to 400 km.The air force is the lead agency for the project and asked the Defence Research and Development Organisation (DRDO) to accelerate development after Operation Sindoor. The defence secretary has announced the success of initial testing.Other systems under development include Akash-NG, the very short-range air defence system (VSHORADS) and a two-tier ballistic missile defence system, whose first phase has been validated.Pakistan has built an organisation and a family of missiles intended to make conventional strikes possible, describing its latest system as hypersonic, although no public flight data is available to substantiate that claim.India, meanwhile, has strengthened both its ability to strike targets at long range and its multilayered defences, which intercepted the earlier attacks. The contest is no longer just about who commands the skies. It is increasingly about who can strike deeper, penetrate defences and sustain the ability to do both.

articles.title: In 2001, Wisconsin mixed fly ash into a reclaimed asphalt road base; its measured stiffness rose 49% by 2002 and 83% by 2003
articles.summary: Discover how Wisconsin successfully recycled failing roadways by incorporating fly ash, resulting in a remarkable 83% increase in pavement stiffness within just two years, showcasing a sustainable approach to infrastructure repair.
articles.body: It is not always necessary to remove the old pavement and lay new quarry material to rebuild a failing road. The state of Wisconsin experimented with a strategy to recycle the current road and strengthen it using coal fly ash, a byproduct of power generation. In October 2001, the road was repaired utilising full-depth reclamation on County Trunk Highway JK in Waukesha County. Rather than cart off the worn asphalt, they pulverised it, blended it with water and self-cementing fly ash, and pressed it into a fresh road base.Follow-up measurements revealed that the base stiffened significantly with age. Estimated modulus increased by 49% in 2002 and by 83% in 2003 from the first 2001 test. The results highlighted the ability of recycled pavement to increase structural strength with time. Subsequent monitoring indicated that cracking and seasonal conditions continued to be relevant problems.How the old pavement became a new baseCounty Trunk Highway JK was a two-lane road in Waukesha County, Wisconsin. The repaired segment was around 1,009 metres long and ran between County Trunk Highways KF and K. The road had challenges with a low-lying position and silty subgrade soils that had contributed to frost-heave problems before the construction.The construction approach was full-depth reclamation (FDR). Crews utilised specialised equipment to crush the current asphalt and the material underneath it in place, creating a blend that could be employed as the basis for the reconstructed pavement. The requirement to take out the old road and re-base it totally with new aggregate was reduced.Class C fly ash was used because it has the ability to generate cementitious characteristics when coupled with water. The ash was included in the recycled pavement material, blended, compacted and allowed to cure before the new asphalt surface was applied. The completed structure utilised the recovered material as a basis instead of treating it as construction waste.The Wisconsin project’s usage of Class C fly ash to stabilise the recycled asphalt base was noted in the 2004 Transportation Research Record study. The early field study showed that the modulus of the base had increased by 49 percent one year after construction, indicating that the material continued to gain strength after the road was opened to traffic.What the measurements of stiffness indicatedThe research team also employed a falling-weight deflectometer to measure the pavement’s response to loading. The equipment drives down the road in a regulated fashion and measures how much the surface yields. Engineers utilise those measurements to evaluate the structural qualities of the pavement layers, such as the modulus of the stabilised foundation material. Modulus is a stiffness parameter. The greater the number, the less a material will deform under a particular load, but the value does not in itself guarantee that an entire road will endure longer or be free of cracking generally.When the first measurements were taken in 2001, the modulus of the fly ash-stabilised base was calculated to be about 1.24 gigapascals or 180,000 pounds per square inch. By 2002, the estimate had climbed to almost 1.84 gigapascals, or 268,000 pounds per square inch. Measurements in 2003 indicated another increase to around 2.27 gigapascals, or 329,000 pounds per square inch. That is an 83% increase compared to the 2001 baseline, not an extra 83% increase above the 2002 number.The ongoing pozzolanic and cementitious processes in the fly ash mix were cited by researchers as the cause for the gains. These reactions may also persist after initial compaction and curing, helping to bond the particles in place and improve the strength of the material. The year-by-year growth in published studies on in-place recycling of asphalt pavements with fly ash is detailed, and the conclusion is drawn that self-cementing fly ash could assist in improving the structural capacity of recovered pavement bases.The calculated coefficient of the structural layer also rose. In 2001 it was about 0.16; it grew to 0.23 in 2002 and reached about 0.245 in 2003. This parameter is used by pavement engineers to evaluate the contribution of a certain layer to the structural capacity of the whole road. Thus, the improvement was obvious in more than one computed measure. The modulus calculated increased considerably. The layer coefficient also showed that the stabilised base was providing greater structural support than it did during the original test.What longer-term surveillance showedThe first results were good, but the longer-term performance of the road was a more difficult story. The first three years were followed by engineers monitoring County Trunk Highway JK to see if the stronger base could continue to perform as well under traffic and changing weather conditions. During the six years of evaluation, the modulus grew in the first three years but was lower in the sixth year compared to the measurement in 2003. Researchers theorised that exposure to freeze-thaw may have damaged the stabilised base. The result indicates why increases observed shortly after construction should not be taken as evidence of a continuing rise in stiffness.Pavement deterioration was also detected during field assessments. Top-down cracking occurred after the third year of construction, followed by thermal cracking and rutting. The high stiffness of the base was thought to be a likely cause of the cracking pattern, but friction between the asphalt surface and the base may also have been a factor in the thermal cracking. In 2008, the American Society of Civil Engineers reviewed the fly ash-stabilised pavement, utilising deflection measures and pavement distress surveys to assess the road's performance over a longer period of time. It showed that a good recycled base still had to perform well with the asphalt layers above it and adapt to seasonal variations.Why this is important is that a road is a multi-layered structure. A firmer base may offer more load-carrying support, but the qualities of the base and surface must be suitable. Engineers have to consider cracking, changes in temperature, moisture and traffic, as well as stiffness measures. The uniformity of the fly ash and the condition of the previous pavement both affect the full-depth reclamation. The material needs to be mixed properly and compressed, and the moisture level and curing conditions can influence the ultimate strength. Other roads could act differently because they don’t have the same soils, traffic, drainage and weather exposure as Waukesha County.The Wisconsin project indicated that recycled asphalt stabilised with Class C fly ash could become stiffer within the first two years of service. The calculated modulus increased by 49% by 2002 and 83% by 2003 over the 2001 baseline, enabling the usage of the material as a structural road base. Later findings added an essential qualification. Increasing stiffness may increase the load-carrying capacity of a pavement but does not prevent cracking or ensure that performance will not vary. The project’s lasting contribution was to show the possibilities of reusing existing pavement and the need to review the whole road system over time.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.summary: Over 50 fighters of the Saudi-led coalition were reportedly killed on Monday after the Houthis fired several ballistic missiles on the Yemeni government
articles.body: Over 50 fighters of the Saudi-led coalition were reportedly killed on Monday after the Houthis fired several ballistic missiles on the Yemeni government military training camp in Shabwa province.The rebels fired at least three ballistic missiles on the al-Alam military camp in the southern province, Reuters reported.The attack also wounded around 70 fighters, AFP reported earlier, with many wounded eventually dying.Footage capturing the aftermath of the strikes pans across a wide stretch of sandy ground where numerous bodies lie scattered, with several body parts, including limbs, blown away and shredded clothes.Debris and what appear to be personal belongings are also visible on the ground.According to AP, the attack was among the deadliest in a recent escalation of fighting that began months ago amid rising tensions in the wider Iran-US conflict.The renewed clashes between the Houthis and forces of Yemen’s Saudi-backed government have broken a 2022 ceasefire that had largely halted fighting in the country’s civil war.According to the Houthi health ministry at least nine people, including five children and two women, were killed during a Saudi-led coalition airstrike on rebel-controlled northern province of Saada.The strike was among several attacks over the weekend that killed or injured more than 30 people, the rebels said.As the fighting continued on Monday, Yemen’s government forces have claimed recapturing Sanamat in Taiz governorate and advanced towards Misrakh following a counteroffensive against Houthi fighters, Al Jazeera reported.One civilian was reported killed and five others wounded in Houthi shelling.Houthi forces have been attempting to encircle Taiz city, a government stronghold where the UN has warned that food supplies are running low. articles.title: Dussehra 2026: Date, Time, Puja Vidhi, Shubh Mahurat and all you need to know
articles.summary: Dussehra, also called Vijayadashami, falls on Tuesday, October 20 this year.
articles.body: Dussehra, also called Vijayadashami, falls on Tuesday, October 20 this year. It’s the day Hindus celebrate the victory of good over evil, and for most families that means morning prayers, a trip to the Ramlila ground by evening, and a crowd staring up at a tall Ravan effigy waiting to be lit. Behind the festival are two stories: Lord Rama’s defeat of Ravana, and Goddess Durga’s defeat of the demon Mahishasura. Which one people think of first depends a lot on where they grew up.Date and shubh muhuratVijayadashami is observed on Dashami, the tenth day of the bright fortnight of Ashwin. Hindu festivals follow the lunar calendar, and local customs vary, so the exact day or hour can shift from one region to another.These are the Drik Panchang timings for New Delhi:Dussehra / Vijayadashami: Tuesday, October 20, 2026Dashami Tithi begins: 12:50 PM, October 20Dashami Tithi ends: 2:11 PM, October 21Vijay Muhurat: 1:59 PM to 2:45 PM, October 20Aparahna Puja time: 1:14 PM to 3:30 PM, October 20Shravana Nakshatra begins: 3:38 PM, October 19Shravana Nakshatra ends: 6:02 PM, October 20Vijay Muhurat is traditionally seen as a good window to begin something important, whether that’s a new job, a purchase or a fresh project. Aparahna, the early-to-mid afternoon, is when Shami Puja and Aparajita Puja are usually performed. Keep in mind that these times are for New Delhi. If you live in another city, look up your local Panchang before planning anything, because the timings will be a little different.Why Dussehra is celebratedThe festival has two origin stories, and neither cancels out the other.The first comes from the Ramayana. Ravana, the king of Lanka, abducted Sita. Rama went after her with his brother Lakshmana, Hanuman and an army of allies, and the war that followed ended with Ravana’s death and Sita’s return. Ravana wasn’t a crude villain in most tellings. He’s described as scholarly, skilled and enormously powerful, which is exactly why his fall is told as a warning about pride. He had everything except the ability to accept he was wrong.The second story is about Durga. Mahishasura was a demon who had grown strong enough to threaten the gods themselves, and none of them could stop him alone. Durga could. After a long battle she defeated him, and Vijayadashami marks that win.The two stories look different, but the lesson is the same. Strength doesn’t make anyone righteous, and power with no restraint usually ends badly for the person holding it.What Ravan Dahan really meansAcross much of northern India, Dussehra ends at dusk with giant effigies of Ravana, often standing beside his son Meghnad and his brother Kumbhakarna, being set on fire. Fireworks go off inside them, the crowd cheers, and kids on their fathers’ shoulders try to get a better look. Plenty of people head home with a box of jalebis afterward.It’s easy to treat it as just a show, but there’s more to it. The burning is a public way of rejecting wrongdoing. In popular retellings, Ravana’s ruin comes from arrogance and from refusing to respect another person’s choices, and many people take the ritual as a nudge to check their own behaviour. Dishonesty, cruelty, misusing authority, assuming that rank means you never have to answer for anything: these are the “Ravanas” most of us actually deal with.Not every region burns effigies, though. In several places the day is about Durga, or about temple ceremonies, and there’s no Ravan Dahan at all.How the festival changes across IndiaDussehra isn’t one celebration. It’s several, and they look very different depending on where you stand.North India: Ramlila performances stage episodes from the Ramayana, often over many nights, and build toward Ravan Dahan on Dussehra. For a lot of children, this is where they first hear the story properly, long before they read it anywhere.West Bengal: Vijayadashami is the last day of Durga Puja, and the mood is closer to a farewell than a victory party. Idols of the Goddess are taken for immersion in many communities. Going by the Panchang timings provided, Bengal observes Vijayadashami on Wednesday, October 21 in 2026.Karnataka: Mysuru is known for its grand Dasara celebrations, a large public affair that draws visitors from well outside the state.Southern and western India: The day is observed through temple rituals, family gatherings and regional customs, many of them quite different from the northern Ramlila tradition.Nepal: The related major festival is called Dashain.Despite the differences, certain things carry across all of these. There’s food, there’s music, there’s theatre, and there are rituals that bring neighbours together. Each generation inherits the same stories and ends up telling them a little differently, which is probably why the festival has lasted this long.The dates in shortMost of India celebrates Dussehra on Tuesday, October 20, 2026. Bengal Vijayadashami follows a day later, on Wednesday, October 21. Whichever day applies to you, the idea at the center stays the same: it’s worth asking what winning actually means, and what choices make it possible.Get the latest movie news, reviews, and celebrity updates. articles.title: In 1928, A.A. Milne wrote letters about Pooh; in 2023, Simon Smith found his father’s attic papers, and rare drafts and drawings sold for £95,000 in 2025
articles.summary: A collection of rare letters, manuscripts, and illustrations related to A.A. Milne's Winnie-the-Pooh sold for £95,000 at auction, bringing new insights and historical importance to the beloved character.
articles.body: In January 2025, a collection of previously unseen letters, manuscripts and illustrations connected to Winnie-the-Pooh creator A.A. Milne sold at auction for £95,000, bringing renewed attention to documents that had remained among a publisher’s private papers for decades. The archive was found by Simon Smith while he was sorting through the attic of his late father, Leslie Smith, who passed away in November 2023. Among the papers was a letter dated March 28, 1928, where Milne jokingly defended Pooh in response to an article in which a newspaper called the bear a “fabulous monster”. The auction was held almost 97 years after the letter was written, even though the papers were discovered in 2023. The collection consisted of original manuscripts, sketches, proof sheets and correspondence intended for the original publisher Methuen & Co., but which eventually ended up in the archives of later publisher Frederick Muller.A publishing archive hidden among family papersThe discovery was made by Simon Smith, who found the materials among the possessions of his father in Malvern, Worcestershire, England. Leslie Smith, who spent most of his life in the publishing industry and founded the publishing house known as Cressrelles, took over the company associated with Frederick Muller. This is the reason why papers pertaining to Frederick Muller, Milne and Shepard were kept by Leslie Smith. Simon told the BBC that the family was unaware of the size of the collection and could have disposed of it.The papers included original sketches for The Christopher Robin Birthday Book, first drafts of Milne’s poem “Wind on the Hill,” and corrected proofs associated with Now We Are Six and The House at Pooh Corner. The archive also includes letters from children's author Enid Blyton and postcards from J.R.R. Tolkien, known for his work on The Lord of the Rings. This added to the historical importance of the archive by providing insight into the connections within the publishing world of that period.The letters behind the famous bearOne of the key documents which are there in the collection is the letter of Milne written to Pooh’s publisher, dated March 28, 1928. In this, Milne reportedly complained about the description of the character in The Observer, “By the way Pooh protests strongly against being called a ‘fabulous monster’ in today’s Observer.” He further added that Pooh would come to the publisher to prove his point. The humorous language in this letter shows how Milne reacted to the description of his fictional character.Some other letters describe the nitty-gritty of the book illustrations. For instance, Milne was reportedly dissatisfied with some of Shepard’s illustrations and wanted them to be changed. In particular, he reportedly wrote to Muller saying, “The illustrator must do new drawings for April and September as the originals are very poor.” Such letters, together with the drafts and corrected proofs, help understand how the author, illustrator, and the publisher worked out the final results.Rare drafts and drawings reach auctionFollowing the discovery, Simon Smith took the archive to Fieldings Auctioneers in Stourbridge, England. Clive Farahar, an expert on books who is well known for his work on the BBC show Antiques Roadshow, helped to value the items. The auction house divided the archive into 34 lots for its January 16, 2025, sale. Its catalogue described the collection as material from the estate of Frederick Muller that had passed down through subsequent ownership.The archive’s reported total was £95,000, according to BBC reporting. It is worth noting that the figure should be distinguished from the £87,470 combined result reported by ITV for the 28 lots specifically related to Winnie-the-Pooh. Among the individual sales, a group of printers’ proofs and annotated material connected to The House at Pooh Corner and Now We Are Six fetched £18,000, while a draft manuscript for The Christopher Robin Birthday Book sold for £9,500. The auction house’s published results confirm those individual prices and state that the overall total, after calculating the standard 26.3% buyer’s premium on top of the £95,000 hammer price, reached £120,000.The collection had caught the attention of buyers from both Britain and the United States. The director of Fieldings, Will Farmer, told the BBC that about two-thirds of the collection would stay in the United Kingdom while the rest of the collection would go to collectors from America. According to Simon Smith, the outcome surpassed his expectations. In an article in the Guardian before the auction, Simon Smith said that he was planning to use the money raised from the sale for research on Milne’s work.You use AI every day. articles.title: After Bronx mother dies in fall while holding her infant, hundreds raise $32,000 on GoFundMe to support baby and family
articles.summary: A GoFundMe campaign established in memory of Nathaly Michelle Ramirez, a 23-year-old mother who died after falling from a 15th-floor balcony in the Bronx,
articles.body: A GoFundMe campaign established in memory of Nathaly Michelle Ramirez, a 23-year-old mother who died after falling from a 15th-floor balcony in the Bronx, New York, has raised more than $32,000 to support her infant daughter and grieving family. The eight-month-old girl survived the fall and was found in her mother's arms, according to reports citing investigators. Police allege that Ramirez and her daughter were pushed from the balcony. The fundraiser, launched on October 8 by Ramirez's mother, Nathaly Minaya, aims to help the family manage unexpected expenses and support the baby. The campaign received hundreds of donations within days of the tragedy, as relatives, friends and strangers came together to help the family through an immense loss.GoFundMe raises $32,000 for Bronx mother's infant daughter and familyThe fundraiser, titled In Memory of Nathaly Michelle Ramirez, was organised by Minaya to support herself and her granddaughter following Ramirez's death. articles.title: UFC star Max Holloway backs Maui wildfire recovery project; housing community has welcomed nearly 900 people
articles.summary: Max Holloway, the former UFC Featherweight Champion from Waiʻanae, Hawaiʻi, launched the Max Holloway Foundation in 2025 to support underprivileged youth
articles.body: Max Holloway, the former UFC Featherweight Champion from Waiʻanae, Hawaiʻi, launched the Max Holloway Foundation in 2025 to support underprivileged youth across the islands. According to UFC, he partnered with the organisation on a global merchandise fundraiser and charitable sweepstakes for HomeAid Hawaiʻi’s Maui Housing Initiative. The money supported Ka La‘i Ola, which UFC describes as Maui’s largest interim housing development for survivors of the August 2023 wildfires. More than 320 families, nearly 900 people, have already moved in. HomeAid Hawaiʻi’s chief executive said UFC’s donation totalled $1.2 million.How Max Holloway’s foundation is helping rebuild Maui after the wildfiresAccording to the Max Holloway Foundation, Holloway has competed in the UFC since 2012 and is a former UFC Featherweight Champion. It describes him as known for his striking, durability and record-setting performances, and as representing Hawaiʻi on the global stage.Holloway remains closely connected to his roots in Waiʻanae, Hawaiʻi. He uses his platform to support local initiatives, youth programmes and families in need. His focus is on creating opportunities for the next generation and helping young people build confidence, resilience and a sense of purpose.How has Holloway helped rebuild Maui through the Ka La‘i Ola housing projectUFC reported on 14 October 2025 that it had joined Hawaiʻi Governor Josh Green, HomeAid Hawaiʻi, state leaders, community partners and families to celebrate the completion of Ka La‘i Ola. UFC describes the site as Maui's largest interim housing development for wildfire survivors. It says the 57-acre community is for people who lost their homes in the August 2023 Maui wildfires, and that more than 320 families, nearly 900 people, have already moved in.According to UFC, which serves as a corporate sponsor of HomeAid Hawaiʻi, it raised funds and awareness through a global merchandise fundraiser and a charitable sweepstakes. UFC states these were run in partnership with Holloway, whom it describes as a Hawaiʻi native and UFC BMF champion. Governor Green thanked Dana White, UFC and Holloway for contributions to HomeAid Hawaiʻi's Maui Housing Initiative, according to the page. HomeAid Hawaiʻi Chief Executive Officer Kimo Carvalho described the $1.2 million donation as coming from UFC and said the organisation was honoured to welcome Dana White, Lawrence Epstein and Holloway to the completion celebration.How did Ka La‘i Ola provide interim housing for Maui wildfire survivorsKa La‘i Ola was built for survivors who were not eligible for federal FEMA assistance, and Hawaiʻi is the first state to deliver interim housing for this population. The project reached substantial completion in less than 18 months, compared with the four to six years such developments typically take. It says families moved in just months after groundbreaking, helped by emergency proclamations that streamlined permitting. Governor Green is quoted as saying partners can build "not just housing, but hope."The project was delivered by the state of Hawaiʻi and its Department of Human Services, working with nonprofit developer HomeAid Hawaiʻi and the Hawaiʻi Community Foundation, alongside many community organisations. It adds that was originally slated for eventual transfer to the Department of Hawaiian Homelands, that this timeline has advanced by 17 years, and that DHHL will take full ownership of the land, infrastructure and homes by 2029. articles.title: A California developer proposed a nearly 1 million-square-foot AI data centre beside homes, promising 1,600 construction jobs; residents fought back, and a judge has now required a full environmental review
articles.summary: A California judge has ordered a complete environmental review of a proposed artificial intelligence data center in Imperial County.
articles.body: A California judge has ordered a complete environmental review of a proposed artificial intelligence data center in Imperial County. The judgement has marked a major victory for the local residents who have spent months fighting a project they believed could affect the water supply, increase emissions and also disrupt life in their community. The facility in question is backed by developer Sebastian Rucci through his company Imperial Valley Computer Manufacturing (IVCM). The facility is said to span nearly 1 millions square feet, making it to be one of the largest AI-focused data centres planned in California. As reported by Guardian, Rucci has argued that the project would help generate more than 1,600 construction jobs and nearly $30 million in annual tax revenue while helping in the establishment of an artificial intelligence infrastructure hub. But the project has now become a flashpoint in the growing national debate over the environmental impact of AI data centres.Judge sends project back to square oneThe data centre was approved by Imperial County earlier this year under an exemption from California's environmental review requirements. But following legal challenges from the City of Imperial and environmental groups, a county judge ruled that the project cannot proceed without undergoing a comprehensive environmental assessment.The decision effectively pauses development and requires officials to evaluate the facility's potential impact on water resources, electricity infrastructure, emissions and surrounding communities before construction can begin. Legal representatives for the City of Imperial said the review process could take a year or longer and would also require consideration of alternative locations.Residents push backResidents say they only learned of the project from a flyer left on doors the day before Thanksgiving last year. Francisco Leal, whose home is across the street from the site, began texting neighbours. Nearly 3,500 people eventually signed a petition against the facility, and state senator Steve Padilla introduced a series of bills aimed at data centres.Residents cited fears of emissions, harm to wildlife such as the endangered desert pupfish, strain on the power grid, noise and scarce water. The centre would need about 750,000 gallons of water a day, Rucci says, drawn from a region that depends on the drought-stricken Colorado River. He denies the project will cause such harms and says its water use is equivalent to a 160-acre farm.“This project was presented as a Noah’s Ark that’s going to come save everybody,” Leal said. “But the community sees this project as a Trojan horse.”The area has the highest poverty rate in California, at close to 20%, and one in five adults is unemployed. “Communities are asking these questions of who benefits and who pays the price,” said Carla Walker of the World Resources Institute.Lawsuits and political fightsOver the past year, more than half a dozen lawsuits have been filed, a temporary 45-day moratorium on data centres was approved, and a recall campaign targets county supervisor Peggy Price, who supported the project. That campaign is ongoing.The city of Imperial sued the county for bypassing public input and environmental review, and the Sierra Club later joined. Rucci’s company, Imperial Valley Computer Manufacturing, countersued in federal court and also sued the local irrigation district over a rejected water application. He filed defamation suits against an activist, a nonprofit and its director, and public-media station KPBS and a reporter. Those three suits were dismissed. He has appealed two of them and is working to reverse the third.At a March county meeting, protesters chanted “no datacenters” and Rucci left early. The county approved the project in April.AI boom fuels race for data centre sitesThe dispute highlights the increasing tension between communities and developers seeking land for AI infrastructure. The rapid growth of artificial intelligence services such as large language models has triggered a construction boom in data centres, which require vast amounts of computing power, electricity and cooling capacity.Developers are increasingly targeting rural and economically disadvantaged regions where large plots of land and power supplies are available. Imperial County, with its industrial zoning and access to significant electricity resources, became an attractive location despite concerns over scarce water resources and environmental sensitivity.According to Rucci, the project would eventually secure access to 330 megawatts of electricity, enough to power a sizeable city.Google link questionedRucci previously suggested the facility could support Google's AI ambitions, claiming to have secured interest from the technology giant for the project. Emails cited in the report indicated the proposed data centre could be used for AI and Gemini-related computing workloads.However, Google denied involvement in the Imperial County project and said it was not part of any data centre development in the area. Rucci acknowledged there was no formal agreement in place.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Meet Niv Agaram, the Indian-origin woman who made JD Vance concede that his rhetoric against H-1B, calling them 'indentured servants' was imperfect
articles.summary: Nivriti Agaram, a graduate of George Washington University, told Vice President JD Vance that her first vote after she became a US citizen was for
articles.body: Nivriti Agaram, a graduate of George Washington University, told Vice President JD Vance that her first vote after she became a US citizen was for Trump-Vance. At a CBS News Town Hall, Niv Agaram told Vance that she voted for him because of border safety, drugs and trafficking issues, and not because she thought immigrants actually take away jobs from Americans. "After seeing ICE behave like military police and then you recently called H-1B visa workers foreign indentured servants -- I think Americans are anything but safe," Niv said, asking why the administration was "scapegoating" immigrants for the issues the government should be solving.JD Vance conceded that his rhetoric against the H-1B visa holders was not perfect, and he did not mean to say it about all H-1B visa holders but a section of them. Explaining the entire issue of companies bringing foreign workers, wrongfully claiming that there are no Americans available for these jobs and then holding the workers almost on a bond, Vance said that when he used the term "indentured servants", it was not to criticize the individuals, but the companies.Vance then cited the Indian origin of his in-laws and said he is not vilifying the immigration system; he just wants to ensure social cohesion. He said if too many people come to the US, even if they are good people, it changes the country in very profound ways. “I don't think it's unreasonable for an American citizen to want to share their community with people they have something in common with,” Vance said. “And I think our immigration system has to build that.Who is Niv Agaram?As she said, Niv's family immigrated to the US around 20 years ago and she became a citizen five years ago. She has been vocal against ICE atrocities and has taken part in anti-ICE protests in Minneapolis. From Washington DC. she flew to Minneapolis to take part in anti-ICE protests. “This is not the America I voted for,” she said at that time to The Free Press.You use AI every day.
